title: Influence of graded dehydration on hyperthermia and cardiovascular drift during exercise
population: Eight endurance-trained cyclists (VO2max 4.72 L/min) cycling 2 h at 62-67% VO2max at 33 C, 50% relative humidity
findings: Four fluid conditions replaced 0, 20, 48 and 81% of sweat loss, producing body-weight losses of 4.2, 3.4, 2.3 and 1.1%.
After 2 h, esophageal temperature, HR and stroke volume differed significantly among trials (P<0.05) except no-fluid vs small-fluid.
Dehydration magnitude was linearly related to the rise in core temperature (r=0.98), the rise in HR (r=0.99) and the decline in stroke volume (r=0.99).
The large-fluid trial attenuated hyperthermia, with forearm blood flow 20-22% higher than with small or no fluid; sweat rate did not differ among trials.
limitations: 1992 study of eight trained male cyclists; r values are group-level across four conditions, not person-level; running not tested.
implications: Drift scales with dehydration: for hot long runs, prompt fluid intake (replace most sweat loss; 81% was best in this study) and treat a late HR rise with uncertain fluid status as a hydration flag before reading it as fitness loss.
Exclude or flag hot, low-fluid long runs when estimating an athlete's durability from HR drift; the 1.1% to 4.2% body-weight loss range gives a rough hydration-confound scale.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (J Appl Physiol 1992 Oct;73(4):1340-50).
